title: "furniture" is developer slang that reached the UI ("new operations and furniture join it", "is setup furniture, not a model")

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:low
labels.description: Mechanical, one file, no new logic (issue-worker-low)

body:
Reported by a user in #866 ("Note the 'furniture join'. Seems like AI is hallucinating"), raised by the maintainer, investigated and filed by an agent. Same kind of problem as #876 ("work offset word").

## What "furniture" means
It is this codebase's internal nickname for the things a setup owns that are neither the part's models nor operations: the setup's stock, its WCS (work offset), its fixtures, machine, post and tool list. The source comments use it everywhere (`crates/app/src/setup.rs`, `schema.rs`, `model.rs`: "setup furniture, never a browser row"; `setup::is_furniture_shape`). It is a fair metaphor in comments. It is not a machining term, and no user can know it.

## Where it reached the user (strings, not comments)
- `crates/ui/src/egui_app/setup_pages.rs:148` - the radio button on a setup's page: **"Active setup - new operations and furniture join it"** (since d017b74b, 2026-11-09). This is the "furniture join" of #866. It means: new operations, and the stock, work offset and fixtures you create, will belong to this setup.
- `crates/ui/src/egui_app/pages.rs:794` - "The Stock and Work-offset pages edit the active setup's furniture."
- Refusals a user or an MCP client can see: `commands/update_model.rs:81` and `commands/repair_model.rs:47` "'{name}' is setup furniture, not a model"; `commands/fixture.rs:91` "'{name}' is setup furniture or CAM data, not a model to mark"; `commands/setup.rs:95` "... that separator belongs to setup furniture"; `commands/setup.rs:109` "'{name}' is reserved for setup furniture".
- `crates/app/src/mcp/model_tools.rs:36` - the `repair_model` tool description (check it and the other MCP descriptions and script API messages for the word).

## Fix
Say what the thing is, in plain words (maintainer, 2026-11-11, on #876: the wording must be English people grasp):
- the radio: e.g. "Active setup - new operations, stock, work offset and fixtures are added to it";
- the hint: e.g. "The Stock and Work-offset pages edit the active setup.";
- the refusals: name the kind, e.g. "'Setup1/Stock' is a setup's stock, not a model" / "is part of a setup (its stock, work offset or fixtures), not a model"; "'{name}' is a name reserved for a setup's stock and work offsets".
Sweep every user-facing string, MCP description and script message for "furniture" (and list what was checked in the PR). Comments and identifiers may keep the word. Update the tests that pin these strings; no snapshot PNG changes; no behaviour change.

Overlap: the contributor's draft PR #875 (for #866) says it rewords 'furniture' on the path it touches. Check what it changed before starting, and do not duplicate it - this issue covers the rest.

Done means: no user-facing string, MCP tool description or refusal contains "furniture"; each says plainly what it refers to; the pinning tests are updated.

title: Theme and colour-vision mode are user preferences, not project state: remember them per user
body:
**What happens now**

The theme is document state. `SetTheme` writes a `ThemeRef` singleton into the world, the project file saves it as an optional `theme` key (`crates/app/src/project/file.rs`, written by `project/wire.rs`), and opening a project sets it again (`project/apply.rs`; no key means Dark). So:

- A new document always opens in Dark.
- Each project carries its own theme. Someone who works in Light has to switch every new project, and a colleague's project opens in whatever theme its author used.
- Changing the theme is an undoable edit to the document, and it marks the project as changed.

**Decision (reporter, vilts, 2026-11-11):** the theme and the colour-vision mode are purely user preferences. They have nothing to do with the project, and both survive program restarts.

**Proposed**

- Keep the chosen theme per user, in the OS config folder, the same way recent files already do (#662, `app::recent`: `%APPDATA%`, `~/Library/Application Support`, `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`; write to a temp file, then rename; a missing or corrupt file starts at the default and says why on the status line, never crashes). Read it at startup and write it when the user picks a theme.
- The project file stops storing the theme. Saving writes no `theme` key. Opening ignores a `theme` key in older files and leaves the user's theme as it is (a compatible read, so no project-file version break is needed for existing documents). Opening a project or File > New never changes the look.
- A missing theme file (a `{"file": path}` preference whose file is gone) keeps the current behaviour: refused by name on the status line, falling back to the built-in default without crashing.
- Theme selection leaves the document's undo history, like the recent-files list (#662: "app PREFERENCE state, not document state"). The pick still goes through one place that validates it (the existing pre-parse in `State::select_theme`), so a corrupt theme is refused at the pick.

**Colour-vision mode too**

The colour-vision mode (`SetColorVision`) is not in the project file and is not saved anywhere, so it resets on every restart. It is kept in the same per-user preference store as the theme, read at startup, and written when the user picks a mode. The startup read still runs the colour-vision gate against the theme it lands on, so a stored mode that fails the gate is refused by name, not applied silently.

**Tests**

The existing theme tests pin the old design and are removed, not updated:
- `project_roundtrip.rs::the_theme_choice_round_trips_and_a_v40_file_means_dark` (the save writes `theme`, and opening applies it)
- `commands_undo.rs::theme_choice_undoes_redoes_and_refuses` (a pick is in the undo history)

Replaced by:
- One project-file test of the new rule: saving writes no `theme` key, and opening an older file that still carries `"theme": {...}` loads cleanly and leaves the user's theme as it was. This guards against a project file overriding the preference again.
- Preference-store tests for theme and colour vision: survives a restart, and a missing or corrupt file starts at the default with a note.

**Done means**

Pick Light, then File > New: the new document is Light. Open a project saved with `"theme": {"named": "dark"}`: it stays Light. Restart the app: still Light. Pick a colour-vision mode, restart: still that mode. Saving a project writes no `theme` key. A corrupt preference file starts in Dark with a status-line note. Tests pin each of these, with the preference store pointed at a temp folder so the suites never touch the real user file.

Labels intended (the filer can't set labels): `enhancement`, `P2`, `effort:medium`, `area:ui`, `source:agent`. Related: #662 (recent files, the store to copy), #698 (light theme), #659.

title: WCS page says the work offset "is set per setup on the Setups page" directly above the dropdown that sets it; "work offset word" is jargon

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:low
labels.description: Mechanical, one file, no new logic (issue-worker-low)

body:
Reported by the maintainer from the properties panel (2026-11-11), investigated and filed by an agent.

## What the user sees
On the WCS node's page:

```
WCS (G54): 52.80, -128.60, 5.00  yaw 0.0
The work offset word is set per setup on the Setups page.
  Work offset  [G54 v]
```

The sentence sends the user to another page for a setting whose dropdown sits on the very next line. And "work offset word" reads as nonsense unless you know that RS-274 calls `G54` a "word".

## Is it invented text? No - it is real text that went stale
- `crates/ui/src/egui_app/pages.rs:648` draws the sentence at the end of `wcs_page`. It came with #342 (commit 6e8deca9, "one WCS per setup; G54-G59 is only the setup's post label"); the code comment above it says the word "is chosen on the Setups page, never here". That was true then.
- #343 then added the picker to this same page: `pages.rs:143-148` calls `wcs_page(ui, state)` and, right after a separator, `setup_wcs_pick::picker(ui, state, name)` ("the WCS node's dialog names its post word too"). The sentence was not removed, so the page now contradicts itself.
- The setting itself is sound: the dropdown queues the undoable `SetSetupWorkOffset`, and the post reads the word through `setup::wcs_slot` (one source). Nothing is wrong with the output; only the text is.

## The same jargon elsewhere
- `crates/ui/src/egui_app/heights_page.rs:108-109` `SETUP_OFFSET_HINT`: "program zero is the setup's WCS: its work offset word is set on the Setups page" (hover on the read-only Work offset row of an operation's heights). True there - that row has no dropdown - but the wording is the same jargon, and since #343 the setting is on the WCS page as well as the Setups page.
- The picker's own hover (`setup_wcs_pick.rs`) says "The G-word the post writes for this setup's WCS ..." - accurate, same jargon.

## Fix
1. Remove the stale sentence from `wcs_page` (and correct the comment above it), or replace it with one line that is true on this page, e.g. "Work offset: the G54-G59 register this setup posts. It does not move the origin."
2. Say "work offset (G54-G59)" instead of "work offset word" / "G-word" in user-facing text: the WCS page, `SETUP_OFFSET_HINT`, the picker's hover. Where a hint points elsewhere, it names the places that really have the control (the WCS page and the Setups page).
3. Sweep the UI strings once for other "... is set on the X page" hints and check each still points at a page that has the control; list what was checked in the PR.
4. Update the structural/AccessKit assertions that pin these strings (`setup_wcs_tests`, `one_wcs`, heights page tests) - no snapshot PNG changes.

Done means: no page tells the user to go elsewhere for a control it shows itself; no user-facing string says "work offset word" or "G-word"; the tests that pin the strings are updated; no behaviour, command or posted output changes.

title: Carry machined stock into a setup turned side-on (90° about X or Y)

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:max
labels.description: New algorithms, formats or open design (issue-worker-max)

body:
Part of #866. Related: #637 (carried stock on the field engine), #586.

**What the reporter wanted:** a plate modelled lying flat; Setup1 machines it flat, Setup2 stands it on its edge (part alignment "turned X -90°") and takes "What Setup1 leaves behind" as its stock. Today that carry is refused by design (`CARRY_TURN_REFUSAL`): the carried body is a two-sided column lattice (`crates/sim/src/stock_sim/carry.rs`, `LatticeTurn`), which can only be re-indexed through flips over X or Y and quarter turns about Z. A side-on turn would need a re-sample at the grid pitch, and the sim refuses rather than guess.

Investigation for #866 confirmed the frame composition is right: `setup_relative::transform_between` uses the RELATIVE turn (`A_to * A_from^-1`), so two setups holding the part alike (both turned X -90°) carry fine (pinned by `setup_stock_source::both_setups_turned_alike_carry_through_the_identity`). Only a real side-on turn between the setups is refused.

**The work:** carry the machined stock through any rigid turn between setups (at least the side-on quarter turns about X and Y - the common "machine the edge" re-clamp), once the carried body lives on the field engine (#637), with the verdicts proven exact enough and the named refusal kept for anything the engine still cannot carry.

**Done means:** Setup1 flat, Setup2 turned 90° about X (or Y) with "What Setup1 leaves behind" simulates, judges gouges and feeds rest/judged stock from the carried body; a pinning test carries a faced plate side-on and checks its volume and verdict.

title: Slow-frame log counts time in a modal file dialog as a 35 s "commands" freeze

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:medium
labels.description: One module or crate, a known pattern (issue-worker-medium)

body:
Part of #866.

**What the reporter saw:** a log line `gpu: slow frame 35098 ms ... slowest phase "commands" 35097 ms` right after importing a STEP, read as a 35-second UI freeze.

**Root cause:** the native file dialogs (`crates/ui/src/file_dialog.rs`, rfd) are modal and synchronous, and they are opened from `State::drain_actions`, inside the frame's "commands" phase (`crates/ui/src/egui_app/shell_window/frame.rs`). The frame watch (`frame_watch.rs`, #74) therefore counted the time the user spent browsing for the file as app work. The log's xdg-desktop-portal warning (the dialog opening) sits right before the slow frame. The STEP itself tessellates off-thread as before; no command ran for 35 s.

**Fix:** the dialog seam times every modal dialog (`file_dialog::take_waited`), and the frame watch takes that time off the frame it happened in (`FrameWatch::excuse`), so a slow frame names real work only.

**Done means:** time spent in a modal file dialog never shows up as a slow "commands" frame, and real work beyond it still does - pinned by `frame_watch::tests::time_in_a_modal_dialog_is_not_a_slow_frame`.

(Not in scope: making the file dialogs asynchronous so the window keeps repainting behind them - the usual modal behaviour, separate if wanted.)

title: Coolant: the machine editor drops an added Air M7, the Carvera post emits M8 from the seeded Flood, and operations can't ask for air

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
From the same Makera Z1 user report (2026-11-11). Makera machines cool with **air, M7**. The user built a Z1 machine file in the editor and tried to add M7 air cooling: **"this was ignored when I saved the profile"**. They asked to be able to:
- disable the default (flood) cooling in the editor and swap it for air; or
- keep both in the profile and choose one per operation.

**What we know from the code (main):**
- A new machine draft is seeded with `"coolants": [{ "name": "Flood", "mCode": "M8" }]` (`crates/app/src/machine/draft.rs:91`).
- `add_coolant` adds a name with **no code** (`draft.rs:147-165`). A coolant whose code is never filled in may then be skipped or dropped. That's likely the "ignored on save".
- `carvera.cps` `coolantCode()` returns the **first `Flood` entry**, else the first entry with a code. So a profile still holding the seeded Flood M8 posts **M8**, even after an Air M7 is added. On a Makera that's the wrong M-code: M8 isn't the air blast.
- Operations choose `CoolantMode` Off / Flood / Mist / Through tool (`crates/post/src/post/coolant.rs`). There's no **Air** mode, and Flood is the silent default, so an op can't ask for "air" by name. The generic posts look the word up in the machine's list and refuse by name when it's missing.

**Fix (sketch; the worker decides the details and records them):**
1. **The editor** can remove or replace the seeded Flood entry, and an added coolant gets its code entered before it's saved. A save never silently drops a coolant; it's refused by name if one is incomplete.
2. **An `Air` coolant mode** (or "air blast", M7 on Makera), selectable per operation, which the posts resolve from the machine's list like Mist.
3. **A machine-level default coolant**, so a machine whose only coolant is air defaults new operations to Air, not Flood.
4. **`carvera.cps`** posts the coolant the operation asked for, not "first Flood". If the machine has no matching entry, it's a named refusal, never a wrong M-code.

Effort: high: it changes posted G-code (safety floor).

**Done means:**
- a machine file with only Air M7 posts M7/M9 for a default operation;
- a profile edited in the GUI keeps its Air M7 after save and reload;
- an operation asking for a coolant the machine lacks is refused by name;
- all pinned.

title: An over-budget STEP mesh is imported at reduced fidelity with only a log line - gouge verdicts on it can pass a real gouge on a convex wall

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Found in the review of PR #839 (#689).

**What happens.** `crates/app/src/geometry/import/step.rs` (`shell_facets`, the refinement loop and the `eprintln!` at about lines 188-207) refines a STEP shell toward its chord target. Since #689 that target is `min(extent/1000, 0.005 mm)`. Refinement stops early once the mesh passes `budget / 8` facets (`MAX_FACETS` = 30 M, less what earlier shells used), or when a pass returns `TooLarge`. The importer then keeps the coarser mesh and only prints "step: tessellated at reduced fidelity ..." to stderr. Nothing in the model, the UI, MCP or the program gate records that the mesh is coarser than the gouge verdict assumes.

A related wrinkle: on the `Err(TooLarge) => break` path, `tol` has already been halved while `refined` is the previous, coarser mesh. The log then under-reports the chord error, and if the halved `tol` reaches the target, it says nothing at all.

**Why it matters, in both directions.** The gouge laws judge the program against these facets with a 0.01 mm verdict. A facet is a chord inscribed in the true surface, so it stands inside the material by its sagitta. That cuts both ways:

- **Concave wall** (a bore or a pocket wall): the facets stand toward the tool. A nominal finish reads as a false gouge, which is the safe side. This was the #689 symptom.
- **Convex wall** (a boss or an outside profile): the facets stand away from the tool, so the mesh wall looks farther off than the real wall. A real gouge up to the mesh's actual chord error can pass the verdict. This is the unsafe side.

AGENTS.md, Prime Directive: "if an operation can only be partly computed, mark it 'incomplete' rather than emit a subtly wrong toolpath", and "Log diagnostics, never silence". A stderr line the user never sees is silence.

This risk is not new. Before #689 every STEP mesh was made at `extent/1000`, which is never finer than what an over-budget model gets now. #689 removes the risk for every model that fits the budget. For an over-budget model it remains.

**Options.**
- (a) The import records the chord error it actually achieved on the model, and the gouge laws tighten their floor by the excess over the 0.005 mm cap for that model. That is stricter, never looser; false gouges on concave walls are the safe side.
- (b) The model is flagged "reduced fidelity" visibly in the UI and MCP. The program gate refuses to post operations judged against it until the user acknowledges it or re-imports with a larger budget.
- (c) Both.

**Recommended: (c).** (a) alone keeps the verdict sound but leaves the user wondering about false gouges. (b) alone relies on an acknowledgement.

Done means: an over-budget import is visible to the user and to MCP; no gouge verdict on such a model can be looser than on a full-fidelity one; and tests pin both, including the `TooLarge`-break path's reported chord error.

title: adaptive growth: the overload fallback picks the largest step on truncated readings and walks it far past the bound

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
What happens: `Planner::step_search` (crates/motion/src/machining2d/adaptive/grow.rs) tries up to 7 growth steps with `walk_until(.., limit = bound)`, which stops at the FIRST reading past the bound. When no step holds, the fallback keeps "the least overload" from those truncated readings. Where the overload sits before the g-dependent front (it does not grow with the step), every try reads the same, the tie goes to the first (largest) step, and that step is then walked whole - far past the reading it was chosen on.

Evidence (release, `HSM_ONE=island hsm_one`, island 60x40/12x12, on d1920031 with the #844 compile break stubbed locally and the growth budget lifted to reach the growth): round the island's NE corner, revs 153-159 read the same first exceedance at every step from 1.88 down to 0.088 mm (e.g. rev 159: 59.5 deg x7), the largest step was kept and walked whole at 57.5 -> 125 deg (79.4 % D at (43.66, 25.81)). This is the 125 deg / 176 breaks round 9 of #7 blamed on the spiral's geometry.

Held fix: branch `issue/7-r10-corner-reading`, e4039ef0 - re-walk each tried step whole and keep the least. Island readings with it: every overloaded revolution reads <= 55 deg (bound ~47.5; worst now at the SW wall, (17.58, 6.01)), the NE-corner overloads are gone. Cost: the growth work on the island doubles (61,971 r, vs ~31,000 before, vs the #13 `WORK_MAX` 30,000), because the smaller steps take more revolutions, and each overloaded revolution adds up to 7 whole walks.

Done means: the fallback chooses the least overload by whole readings (a pinning test where the truncated reading ties and the whole reading does not), with the #13 growth budget kept honest (either the extra walks are not charged as growth work, the re-walk is bounded, or WORK_MAX is recalibrated on the fixtures with the band refusal re-timed); goldens that move are listed.

Found while working #7 (round 10). Part of the #7 picture, but a defect on any growth plan with an overloaded revolution.

title: Synthetos TinyG post processor (3-axis mill)

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
### What are you trying to do

Post 3-axis milling programs for machines running [Synthetos TinyG](https://github.com/synthetos/TinyG) (the TinyG v8 board, ATxmega192A3), the other grbl-family hobby controller. CamCraft has no TinyG post; #710's grblHAL post is the closest, but TinyG understands a smaller set again: no canned cycles at all (G81-G89 are rejected), no G41/G42, no G84, `M6` only records the tool, tool numbers stop at 31, and the serial input acts on `!`, `~` and `%` wherever they stand in a line.

The firmware's `edge-next` branch (build 450.03) is what I maintain and test on real boards, so posted programs can be checked against its own parser and planner off the board, and on a board after that.

### How you imagine it working

A new `assets/posts/tinyg.cps` (3-axis mill), structured like `grblhal.cps` and specced from TinyG's public wiki ("Gcode Support", "Homing and Limits", "Flow Control and Footers", "Inch and Millimeter Units Mode") and the LinuxCNC G-code reference TinyG states it follows (behaviour only; the firmware source is GPL and is not read for this), plus a generic `assets/machines/tinyg-3axis.mch`.

What the post respects (each checked against the wiki and by replaying the output through the edge-next parser and planner):
- **Drilling as plain moves**: a CYCLE record writes nothing; the hole's expanded chain posts, with the dwell as `G4 P<seconds>` at the hole bottom. Tapping is refused by name (no G84, no spindle sync).
- **Tool change**: Z lift, then `T<n> M6` alone on its line, then `M0` on the next - M6 moves nothing on TinyG, so the stop is the operator's change. Tools T1-T31; a larger number is refused by name.
- **Header `G21|G20 G17 G90 G91.1 G94 G64`**: the words M30 does not reset on TinyG. No `%`, O word or N numbers; no tool length word (G43.1/G49 belong to the operator or sender, as #710 decided for grblHAL).
- **Z lift as grblHAL's**: `G53 G0 Z<safe_retract>` only when the machine file states it; otherwise the work-offset clearance, refused by name when unknown or not above the stock. No G28/G30.
- **Comments** drop `!` (feed hold), `~` (cycle start), `%` (queue flush) and the other characters the serial input acts on; lines stay under 191 bytes.
- Refused by name: control/wear compensation, going home, tilted moves; probing is refused by the engine (no parameters or expressions on TinyG).

**Done means:** `tinyg.cps` and the machine file ship in `assets/`; the post is in the conformance list (tap refused), `EXTENSIONS` and the cross-post tests like `grblhal`; a `tinyg_post` test and goldens under `crates/app/tests/golden/nc/tinyg/` cover contour, pocket, face, slot, trace, drill, peck and tool change; every golden replays through the edge-next firmware's parser and planner with no refused line.

Related: #710 (grblHAL post; this stacks on #715, which it extends the same lists as), #714.

title: A tool body is judged as two different shapes: the fixture laws sweep its band stack, the reach laws its enclosing cylinder - the simulation can only draw one

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Found while working #743 part 1 (the simulation draws the tool as the revolved outline the laws judge).

**What happens.** A milling tool with a body (an imported mesh, #368, or a drawn spun holder, #93) is read by the collision laws in two different shapes:

- the fixture laws (`fixture_struck`, `operation::generate` -> `tool_body::stack` -> `verify::steel_stack`) sweep the body's **band stack** - its revolved envelope, up to 32 coaxial bands;
- every law that reads one holder cylinder off `ToolGeom` - law (c), the shank/holder reach against the part and stock walls in `crates/sim/src/verify/reach.rs` (`cx.tool.holder_radius`, `cx.tool.holder_len`), and the probe stack in `verify/probe.rs` - reads the tool `tool_body::judged` returns: the single cylinder **enclosing** the body (`HolderProfile::enclose`): the holder at the body's widest radius from the shank top to the body's top, and the shank widened to the widest the body reaches beside it.

Both are conservative (never smaller than the body), so no collision is missed. But they are not the same shape: for a stepped body (a narrow nose under a wide flange) the enclosing cylinder is the flange's radius all the way down to the shank top.

**Why it matters.** #743 asks that the simulated tool be "the same profile the collision laws judge, so what you see is what is checked". The simulation (PR for #743 part 1) draws the band stack, the tighter of the two and the one the laws that name a fixture collision read. A reach warning from law (c) can therefore fire where the drawn holder is visibly clear of the wall: the user sees a nose 15 mm from the axis, the law judged 40 mm.

**Evidence.** `crates/app/src/tool_body.rs` (`judged`, `stack`), `crates/tools/src/holder_profile.rs` (`enclose`, `stack`), `crates/sim/src/verify/reach.rs` lines 38-45. `crates/app/tests/tool_spun_profile.rs` already pins the two readings side by side (the enclosing cylinder's radius equals the widest band).

**Options (not decided here).**
1. Law (c) and the other single-cylinder laws read the band stack too (changes verdicts: fewer false reach warnings; under the safety floor, needs its own goldens).
2. Keep the laws; a reach warning from an enclosed body says so in its text ("judged by the cylinder enclosing the body, Ø…"), and the simulation can show that cylinder when such a warning is selected.

Not touched by #743 part 1 - that PR is display only and changes no verdict.

Done means: either every law that judges a tool body reads the same shape the simulation draws (with tests pinning the changed verdicts), or the difference is stated in the warning text and shown on demand, with a test that the drawn shape and the named judged shape agree for each law.

Part of #743.

title: Field march: phi == 0 on a cell centre returns a mid-cell height - under-reports material

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Found by the #817 review (https://github.com/NeoTech/Camcraft/pull/817#pullrequestreview-5857229231). The bug is already on main, and it doesn't need a flip.

**Where:** `crates/sim/src/stock_sim/march.rs:241-242`. The arm `phi == 0.0 => Read::Top(z)` treats a probe value of exactly zero as "the probe landed on the surface". But the probe's magnitude belongs to the whole cell, so `phi == 0` only means the cell's **centre** lies on a stock plane. The march then returns whatever height it reached inside that cell.

**Scenario:** a plate from -6.25 to 0 at cell 0.5, so -6.25 sits on a cell centre, with a flat slot at -6.0.
- Expected: `[-6.25, -6.0]` is still material.
- Actual: the read is `Material { top: -6.25, floor: -6.25 }`, so 0.25 of steel reads as air.

That feeds `march_verdicts` and `columns`. The field engine isn't the default engine, so this is latent today, but it's a silent under-report.

**Fix:** treat `phi == 0` as "this cell's centre is on a surface": refine from the cell, or answer `Unreadable`. Pin it with a fixture whose stock plane sits on a cell centre. The mirrored arms in #817's `march_up.rs` get the same fix there.

Done means: no read under-reports material when a stock plane sits on a cell centre; pinned.

# Part alignment from two perpendicular edge picks: the picks define the full 3D frame

## What

The axis-pick panel (Setup > align) refuses an out-of-plane pick: "the
+Y pick runs (nearly) along the work plane's normal (Z)". But two
perpendicular picks — an edge for +X, an edge for +Y — already define a
complete 3D frame: the +X pick's direction maps to world +X, the +Y
pick's to world +Y, and Z+ follows by the right-hand rule (the user's
rule: the directions decide where Z+ points). Today's `turn_in_plane`
(`app/src/pick/axis.rs`) only spins about the work plane's normal and
throws that information away.

## The law (from the discussion with the user)

- Pick two lines (edges or two-point picks) that run across each
  other: the +X pick's direction maps to world +X, the +Y pick's to
  world +Y, and the part's Z+ lands where the right-hand rule puts it
  (R(d_x) x R(d_y) = +Z).
- The pivot is the parts' centre (the part stays on its spot of the
  table) — the ORIGIN question is deliberately out of scope here: the
  work offset is placed separately, as it is today.
- Nearly-perpendicular picks: the primary axis lands exactly, the
  secondary is orthogonalized against it; picks that run (nearly)
  along each other refuse by name (no frame can be read from them).
- Flip flags keep their meaning (a reversed edge flips its direction).
- The landing is proven before the command stores anything (the
  primary runs along its axis, the secondary within the skew it came
  with, the frame right-handed) — never a silently wrong frame.

## Scope

- `pick/axis.rs`: `align_from_axes(world, setup, axes)` — the general
  construction, which subsumes the in-plane turn for in-plane picks.
- `commands/setup_align.rs`: the `AlignPartToSetup` constructor for it.
- The UI call site (`ui/src/state.rs`, the axis-pick panel's apply)
  switches from `turn_in_plane` to the general path — the same panel,
  the same picks, now with the full meaning.
- `turn_in_plane` stays for its in-plane callers; the general path must
  reproduce its results for in-plane picks (subsumption, pinned
  numerically).

## Done means

- The user's exact case aligns: a part whose +Y edge runs along world
  (0, 0, -1) and +X edge along (-1, 0, 0) lands with +Y along +Y, +X
  along +X and the cross-normal up — one pick round, no plane-first
  step.
- In-plane picks behave exactly as `turn_in_plane` did (existing suites
  green: turn_pivot, plane_align, the setup axis tests).
- Numeric tests: out-of-plane perpendicular picks, subsumption for
  in-plane picks, near-perpendicular skew, parallel picks refused by
  name, flips honored, undo restores.

title: xtask: the test scanner counts braces inside string literals, so gate test misses tests and quick picks the wrong fn

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:medium
labels.description: One module or crate, a known pattern (issue-worker-medium)

body:
What happens: `cargo xtask gate test <name>` reports `no #[test] fn matches '<name>'` for a test that exists, and the quick tier can attribute a changed test to the wrong function.

Repro on upstream/main (any OS):

```
cargo xtask gate test the_library_folder_is_the_override_else_a_sibling_of_machines --dry-run
# no #[test] fn matches 'the_library_folder_is_the_override_else_a_sibling_of_machines'
cargo xtask gate test a_bad_library_is_refused_whole_by_name --dry-run
# ok - 1 step
```

Cause: `xtask/src/scan.rs` `test_fns` finds each test's end by counting `{` and `}` characters on every line, including those inside string and char literals. In `crates/app/tests/fixture_library.rs`, `a_bad_library_is_refused_whole_by_name` (line 78) calls `refuse("{", "bad JSON")`. The unbalanced `{` in that string keeps the depth above zero past the test's real closing brace, so its span swallows the next test, `the_library_folder_is_the_override_else_a_sibling_of_machines` (line 111). That test never appears in the scan.

Effects:
- `gate test <name>` cannot run the swallowed test, by name or substring, with or without `--exact`/`--binary`.
- The quick tier picks "the changed #[test] fns of a changed suite" from these spans. A diff inside the swallowed test is attributed to the test before it, so quick can run `--exact` on the wrong fn and report green without running the changed test. (Seen on PR #761: quick reported `app fixture_library (1 fn)` ok while the changed test was the swallowed one.)

Fix direction: skip `{`/`}` inside string literals (`"..."`, with `\"` escapes), raw strings (`r"..."`, `r#"..."#`), char literals (`'{'`) and `//` comments when counting depth. Pin it with an xtask unit test whose fixture has a test containing `"{"` followed by a second test that must be found with the right span.

Done means: both repro commands find their test; the new xtask unit test pins a brace-in-string fixture; the quick tier attributes a change in the second test to the second test.

# One machining-frame seam: OpFrame composes part_alignment and TiltedFrame

## What

The part-alignment machinery (#326) and the per-operation tilt frame (the
3+2 index, M5.1 B) both exist and both work — but only separately.
`setup_align::generation_problem` allows generation in an aligned setup for
exactly four kinds (Face, 2D Contour, 2D Pocket, 2D Adaptive), and tilt
inside an aligned setup is refused outright. Every other planar kind,
picks, and area controls are refused by name. The refusals are a
verification gap, not a mathematical one: the two mechanisms compose as
plain function composition.

This issue builds ONE seam — `OpFrame`, `crates/app/src/operation/frame.rs`
— that composes the two existing mechanisms and becomes the single door
the generators' world reads go through. No generator rewrites: the motion
generators take data (facets, regions, heights); only the app read/wrap
seam moves.

## The frame contract

Coordinate systems:

- **D** — document frame (as modelled). Part entities carry their
  `Location` in D.
- **S** — setup frame: the table frame, also the world the CL stream and
  the post speak. Stock, WCS and fixtures are setup FURNITURE — stored in
  S already (#326's law; their world reads are correct and stay untouched).
- **L** — local machining frame: XY = the cutting plane, +Z = the tool
  axis. Exists only when the op tilts.

Point maps (right-to-left application, the `setup_align::compose`
convention):

- D → S: `A` = the setup's `part_alignment`, baked into part geometry
  reads (`facets_in` and siblings). Never inverted — the CL never maps
  back to D.
- S → L: `T` = `TiltedFrame` from `op.params.tilt()` (`to_local`), applied
  AFTER the alignment read: `p_L = T(A(p_D))`.
- L → S (CL out): `T.to_world`, the tilt's inverse. The whole CL stream
  wraps through `TiltedFrame::world_path`; identity when no tilt exists.

Layers stay separate (never a fourth):

1. part_alignment — setup, physical (how the part is clamped)
2. WCS — program zero (translation today)
3. operation tool orientation — the `Tilt` param

Machine-side relations remain derived internal transforms composed from
these; no user-facing SCS, no second offset frame.

## Design conditions (from the plan review)

1. **Heights and bounding boxes resolve against fully transformed
   geometry** (local bounds of `T(A(f))`), never a bare `z − origin.z`
   shift — a Z shift is not generally correct for an arbitrarily tilted
   plane. `OpFrame`'s height and AABB reads implement this from day one.
2. **Machine capability gates are preserved and pinned by tests**: a
   tilted orientation never silently posts as plain XYZ when the machine
   cannot reach it. The post's tilted-record refusals (non-RTCP, no
   rotary) keep their verdicts.
3. **Stepwise integration**: Phase 1 wires the seam behind the four
   currently-supported kinds, byte-identical. Refusals lift only as their
   numeric tests land: picks in aligned setups next, then further 2D/3D
   families, alignment × tilt last.

## Phases

- **Phase 1 (first branch)**: `OpFrame` + the four kinds through it,
  behavior byte-identical; the seam's math pinned by unit tests (identity,
  90°/180° alignment, alignment × tilt composition, transformed picks,
  local heights on tilted planes, AABBs under arbitrary rotation, CL
  back-transform, tool direction, capability gates, byte-identity).
- **Phase 2**: the selection walk reads picked parts through the seam
  (`facets_in`); picks in aligned setups verified. Tilt × picks stays
  refused.
- **Phase 3**: `verified_kind` extended kind by kind (whole-model 3D
  kinds first), each with a pinned numeric test; area controls; then tilt
  × alignment.
- **Phase 4**: re-evaluate #760 (rotated-offset carry) on top of the
  unified seam — normal 3-axis work needs alignment coverage, not offset
  rotation.

## Done means (Phase 1)

- `crates/app/src/operation/frame.rs` exists with the contract above;
  `collect_job` reads geometry/heights for the four kinds through it.
- The mandatory test list above is green.
- Existing aligned-setup tests (#326's) and goldens pass unchanged —
  byte-identical output.
- No refusal lifted, no post change, no generator change.

Related: #326 (part alignment), #316 (setup-to-setup transform), #315
(rotation refusal at the post), #760 (rotated-offset carry — re-evaluated
in phase 4, untouched by this issue's branches).

User-reported on main 5fd45923: align a setup's WCS with 3-2-1 on a turned part → the WCS is right in the display, toolpath and machining plane do not follow. Not yet pinned by a test.

**Fix (step 3 of #315, owed)**

Carry the rotation end-to-end, as a user parameter with a default:

- generation and heights compute in the offset's frame, so toolpath and machining planes follow the alignment, and
- the post either bakes rotated coordinates into the program or emits the control's own rotation where the machine declares it (Fanuc G68 / G68.2, Siemens CYCLE800 / ROT, Heidenhain PLANE / CYCL 10 — public control documentation only; a G54 register is translation only on every control).

Interim, if the full carry is not taken at once: the 3-2-1 flow should say at alignment time that a rotated offset will not post (the refusal currently arrives only at the post gate), or steer to part alignment (#330, #746).

**Done means**

A part aligned with a rotated work offset machines in that frame: toolpath, height planes and posted program all carry the same rotation, pinned against a hand-computed program — or the alignment refuses with a clear message before any toolpath exists. Never a display that shows a frame nothing machines.

**Related**: #315 (the shipped refusal), #187 (3-2-1 alignment), #330 / #746 (part alignment, the alternative path), #701 (will create rotated offsets from feature roles and needs this to machine them).

title: Tool and holder bodies as a spun profile: show them revolved in simulation, and turn an imported STEP body into an editable half-profile (DXF with a centreline)

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:max
labels.description: New algorithms, formats or open design (issue-worker-max)

body:
Requested by the maintainer.

## 1. Simulation shows the tool and holder as spun profiles
While simulating, draw the **tool and its holder as revolved bodies**: the half-profile spun about the spindle axis, at the tool's position and orientation each frame. Today's simulation doesn't show them as solids. Use the same profile the collision laws judge (the revolved envelope, #368), so what you see is what is checked.

## 2. Imported tool bodies and holders become an editable half-profile
When a tool body or holder is imported as **STEP**, convert it to a **2D half-profile on a centreline** (the meridian of the revolved envelope: radius against height along the tool axis). Store it as a **DXF**, with the centreline as its own entity/layer, so the profile can be edited (in the spun-profile editor, #93) and re-exported.

- Only the half-profile is editable, and the body is always its revolution about the centreline.
- Conversion should be conservative: the profile is the outer envelope (max radius at each height), never smaller than the solid, so collision checks stay safe. Non-revolved features (flats, coolant holes, the holder's drive slots) are enveloped, never cut away. Say so in the UI.
- Refuse by name when the STEP body has no clear axis (axis detection/alignment: #370) instead of guessing one.
- A tool/holder can also be **imported directly as a DXF half-profile** (a centreline plus an open profile on one side of it).
- DXF read/write is our own, written from the published DXF reference (entities `LINE`, `ARC`, `LWPOLYLINE`, layers). The minimum needed is lines and arcs, with a named refusal for anything else (splines, unclosed profiles that cross the centreline).

## Related
- #93 spun (revolved-profile) design editor for tool and holder shapes: the editor for these profiles.
- #361 import vendor STEP tool models; #368 a vendor holder judged by its revolved envelope (closed); #370 align a vendor STEP by its tool coordinate systems; #371 pick tip and axis on an imported body (closed).
- Fixtures get the same treatment in a sibling issue.

## Done means
- The simulation draws the tool and holder as revolved solids from their profiles (structural/paint assertion where possible, hand-tested by the maintainer; no snapshot PNG changes).
- Importing a STEP holder produces a DXF half-profile with a centreline, and the envelope encloses the original solid (a test samples the STEP mesh and checks every point lies inside the revolved profile).
- A DXF half-profile imports as a tool/holder body; malformed DXF (no centreline, spline, crossing profile) is a named error in a test, never a panic.
- Round trip: STEP → DXF → body → DXF is stable within tolerance.

title: Generator refusals print millimeters in inch documents

labels.name: claimed
labels.description: An agent is working on this - see the claim comment

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: effort:medium
labels.description: One module or crate, a known pattern (issue-worker-medium)

body:
## What's wrong

`docs/decisions/578-units-in-errors.md` split the millimeter-speaking strings into tiers and lensed the transient ones (#590). The tier it listed under **Considered and dropped** is still open, and it is the tier a user actually reads when an operation refuses:

> Generator refusals in `operation/circle_fit` and the `operation::*` generate paths, and the pure-crate `Display` refusals (`tools`: `spun`, `holder_profile`, `lathe_holder`, `lathe_insert_zone`; `motion`: `descent`, `probing`): these live below the app - pure functions and pure-crate types with no world and no unit in scope. Threading a `Unit` through those APIs for a handful of refusal sentences is a wide signature change with no lens to hang it on.

So in an inch document the fields all read inches and the refusal banner still says millimeters. It is worse than a missing suffix: several sentences *hardcode the word* "mm", so the text is not merely unit-blind, it is wrong.

## Where

The lens is `app::units::of(world)` over the pure formatters in `geometry::units` (`len`, `feed`, `area`, `vol`). Every site below builds its sentence without one:

**App generate paths** (`crates/app/src/operation/`)

| site | sentence |
| --- | --- |
| `material.rs:221`, `:224` | `no material at z = {z:.3}` - no unit at all |
| `area.rs:100`, `:193` | `the part fills the whole selection at Z {z:.3}` |
| `drill_reach.rs:73` | `is {depth:.3} mm deep from the stock surface; tool {name}'s flute reaches {flute:.3} mm` |
| `drill_reach.rs:201-204` | `cycle at ({:.3}, {:.3}) is {depth:.3} mm deep ... past tool {name}'s {flute:.3} mm flute, and its shank dia. {shank_d:.3} does not fit the dia. {} hole` |
| `circle_fit.rs:67` | `deviation {dev:.3} mm at ({:.3}, {:.3})` |
| `contour_open.rs:238-240` | `the open boundary's offset of {d:.3} mm folds onto itself` |
| `cross_stock.rs:284-287` | `cross-drill rapid {i} stops {got:.3} mm out along its hole's line ... ({need:.3} mm)` |

**Pure-crate refusals**

| site | sentence |
| --- | --- |
| `motion/src/machining2d/face.rs:329` | `{what} {step} mm over {span:.3} mm needs more than {MAX_PASSES} passes` |
| `motion/src/drilling/axial.rs:119` | `the drill is {tool_d} mm across, the bore at ({}, {}) is modeled {} mm` |
| `motion/src/finishing3d/params.rs:267` | `3D finish {name} {s} mm reaches the scallop ceiling: passes a ball diameter ({d} mm) apart` |
| `tools/src/spun.rs:79`, `:90` | `shorter than {MIN_SEGMENT} mm`, `({MAX_BODY_RADIUS} mm from the axis, {MAX_BODY_HEIGHT} mm long)` |
| `tools/src/holder_profile.rs:94` | `larger than any tool a spindle carries (500 mm from the axis, 2000 mm long)` |
| `tools/src/lathe_holder.rs:95-97` | `farther than 2000 mm from its tip`, `more than 50.8 mm from the lathe body`, `within 25.4 mm of it` |
| `tools/src/lathe_insert_zone.rs:48` | `reaches {reach:.3} mm from the tip along {axis}, past the {cap:.3} mm one insert can` |
| `motion`: `machining2d/descent`, `machining3d/descent`, `probing` | same shape, named by the decision doc |

## Why it matters

AGENTS.md treats a refusal as data the user acts on, and #261 part 2 already went out of its way to make refusals *locatable* rather than readable as coordinates. A refusal in the wrong units is the same failure from the other side: the sentence tells an inch user to "raise the clearance" against a number that is 25.4x off from what every field on their screen shows.

## Two ways to fix it, and why they are cheaper than they look

1. **Structured refusals** - store the numbers, format at display, the way `sim::verify::Warning` already does. This is the pattern the decision doc already picked for tier 2, so it lands once and covers both tiers' persisted/transient split.
2. **An additive `Unit` argument** on the pure-crate formatters - the decision doc's own closing line: "the pure-crate Displays want a `Unit` argument, additive once anyone wants it."

Neither is as wide as the doc feared, because `GenError` already carries structured data through a frame boundary: `GenError::At { msg, at }` stores a `Point3` and `GenError::map_location` maps it to world *before the UI sees it* (`motion/src/machining2d/gen_error.rs`). A refusal that carries `{ depth_mm, flute_mm }` and formats at display time rides that same already-solved rail, and the app's `run_job` is already the place that knows the world's unit.

The `mm`-hardcoded sentences are the part worth fixing first regardless of which shape is chosen: they can move to `units::len`-style formatting at display time without any new type.

## Pinning it

The `len`/`feed`/`area` law (mm mode byte-identical, inches = the mm precision plus extra decimals) makes this pin-testable the way #590 pinned the gouge clause. `blind_floor::the_gouge_clause_speaks_the_document_s_units` is the template: same world, inch lens, assert the sentence divides by 25.4, says "in", and never says "mm"; and an untouched mm pin proving the mm strings did not move.

One caveat for whoever takes it: the pure-crate refusals that quote *constants* rather than user numbers (`spun`'s `MIN_SEGMENT`, `holder_profile`'s 500/2000 mm spindle ceilings, `lathe_holder`'s 25.4/50.8 mm insert limits) are the MACHINE's/catalog's numbers, not the document's, and the decision doc already ruled that class separate ("the `.mch` grammar has its own unit story"). This issue is about the sentences quoting numbers the user typed into fields that already ride the lens.

body:
Add machine definitions, and the post they need, for Sienci Labs' AltMill CNC routers, driven by the SLB-EXT controller. **There are three sizes:**

| | AltMill 2×4 | AltMill 4×4 | AltMill 4×8 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Work area (X × Y) | ~25 × 49 in | ~49 × 49 in (1265 × 1251 mm) | ~49.8 × 104 in (1265 × 2640 mm) |
| Z travel | ~5.5 in | ~5.5 in (one page: 174 mm) | ~210 mm |
| Max cutting speed | ~590-600 IPM | ~590-600 IPM | ~1,000 IPM Y, ~590 IPM X |
| Spindle | none included: 80 mm mount; optional 2.2 kW ER20 spindle, or the 2.2 kW ATC spindle | as 2×4 | as 2×4 |
| Rotary (optional) | Vortex rotary axis on the SLB-EXT's A output | as 2×4 | as 2×4 |
| Motion | NEMA 23 closed-loop steppers | as 2×4 | as 2×4 |

The figures come from Sienci's product and resources pages, which disagree with each other in places (the 4×4's Z: 5.5 in vs 174 mm; X and Y speeds). Confirm each figure against Sienci's current spec page or manual before committing a `.mch` (see Done means).

**Controller:** the SLB-EXT is a 32-bit board running **grblHAL**, usually driven by Sienci's gSender. That makes this post a grblHAL dialect, built on the grblHAL post in #710 (PR #715) rather than written from scratch.

**No new post file.** The AltMill machine files use `grblhal.cps` from #710, the way all the Tormach mills share `tormach.cps`. A separate `altmill.cps` is added only if something below cannot be a machine-file setting or a grblHAL post option. As of PR #715, the grblHAL post already does what an ATC needs: a plain `T<n> M6` on a line of its own, no G49 (the controller's measured tool length is kept), a `G53 G0 Z` lift when the machine file states `safe_retract` (the AltMill homes), and the first move after a change goes to XY before Z.

**Requirements** (on the machine files, or as small additions to the grblHAL post):
- **Tool change:** the most AltMill-specific part. The post must not depend on the sender: AltMill owners use gSender, and also alternatives such as ncSender. Two modes:
  - *Manual*: the sender intercepts `M6` and runs its own tool-change routine (pause, probe, and so on).
  - *ATC (firmware-handled)*: a `TC.macro` on the SLB-EXT runs `M6 Tn` inside grblHAL, which is transparent to the sender. This covers Sienci's ATC spindle and the **RapidChange ATC** ([rcatc-scripts-grblhal](https://github.com/greilick-industries/rcatc-scripts-grblhal): `TC.macro` runs on every `M6` with a valid tool, settings in `P200.macro`, grblHAL core 20240506 or newer).
  - In both modes the post emits a plain `M6 Tn` on a line of its own, as #710 already plans, with the length offset on the next line. It adds no sender-specific comments or macros, because some gSender versions reportedly rewrite `M6T1` even in passthrough.
  - A post option picks manual or ATC. With ATC, the machine file states the rack's pocket count and which tool numbers it holds, and any other tool is a manual change or a refusal by name. The tool length comes from the ATC's own measurement, so the post does not ask for a manual touch-off after an ATC change.
- **Units:** most AltMill users work in inches. The post honours G20/G21 from the setup and never mixes them.
- **Spindle:** the spindle is bought separately, so the machine file carries a default spindle (the 2.2 kW ER20, 24,000 rpm max, to be checked against Sienci's kit page) that the user can change. `S` words are clamped to the stated range, or refused by name if out of range.
- **Rotary (Vortex):** an A-axis rotary along X on the SLB-EXT's dedicated A output (closed-loop Vortex, gSender's "4th Axis Mode"). The older "Rotary Mode", which drives the rotary through the Y output, is not supported and is refused by name. Indexing and wrapping follow #714 and wait on it.
- **Out of scope:** laser (LaserBeam) and plasma add-ons.

**Done means:**
- `assets/machines/sienci-altmill-2x4.mch`, `sienci-altmill-4x4.mch` and `sienci-altmill-4x8.mch` exist, with travels, axis speeds, the default spindle and the rotary option. Every figure is sourced from Sienci's spec page or manual and cited in the decision file.
- All three are registered in `posting::MACHINES`, with tests in the style of the Tormach machine tests.
- The AltMill machines post through `grblhal.cps`, with goldens under `crates/app/tests/golden/nc/grblhal/` for a small pocket with a tool change on an AltMill machine, in both inch and mm. With an ATC rack stated, a tool outside the rack is handled as above. Any change needed in `grblhal.cps` keeps its existing goldens byte-exact.
- Without #714, any A word is refused by name. Once #714 lands, the Vortex is covered by its indexing goldens.
- The post passes a sender run and a real-machine dry run before it is trusted. I have an AltMill with an SLB-EXT, a RapidChange ATC and ncSender, and can run the goldens on that setup (ATC mode, ncSender).

Depends on: #710 (grblHAL post). Related: #714 (grblHAL 4th axis), #707 (similar machine + post request).

title: Picking: only feature edges, feature points and faces are pickable, never tessellation edges or hidden geometry - one rule for the whole app

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Reported by the maintainer (filed by an agent), 2026-11-10.

## What happens
1. **Tessellation edges are pickable.** The selector lets you pick edges between the mesh's own triangles (at a model's vertices, inside flat faces and along smooth curves). Those aren't real model edges, and no feature should ever be built on them.
2. **Picks go through the model.** In some cases, the "select through" behaviour picks an edge (or a vertex) on the far side of the model, hidden from the user, instead of what's under the cursor.
3. **Inconsistent everywhere.** Face, vertex and edge picking behave differently from page to page: setup alignment, operation geometry, fixture mates, the WCS/origin picks, MCP picks. Users can't build a mental model of what a click will select.

## What should happen - one picking rule, used everywhere
- **Faces:** a face is a welded face, i.e. a smooth patch of triangles merged across soft edges (the `features`/`area` patches MCP's `list_features` already reports). Clicking anywhere on it picks the whole face, never a single triangle.
- **Edges:** only **feature edges** are pickable: edges where two welded faces meet at a real crease, plus open boundary edges of a sheet. Edges between triangles of the same welded face (flat-face triangulation, facets of a smooth cylinder) are never pickable. Chains follow feature edges only.
- **Points:** only **feature points** are pickable: corners where feature edges meet, the end points of open feature-edge chains, and (where a mode asks for it) arc/circle centres derived from a round feature edge. Interior mesh vertices are never pickable.
- **Visible first, never through:** a pick resolves to the front-most visible surface under the cursor (the same depth the viewport draws, perspective and ortho). An edge or point is pickable only if it is visible there (not occluded by the model, within a small screen-space tolerance of the front surface). Nothing on the far side is picked unless the user explicitly turns on a "pick through" mode, which is off by default and shown as such.
- **Snapping order near a feature:** within the pick radius, prefer point, then edge, then face, but **only** among the kinds the current tool accepts (e.g. plane alignment is faces only after #554; axis by edge or two points takes edges/points). A tool that doesn't accept edges never snaps to one.
- **One implementation:** a single picking service in the app layer (feature graph: welded faces, feature edges, feature points; visibility test against the depth the viewport uses) that every UI picker (`plane_pick`, `edge_pick`, `vertex_pick`, `axis_pick`, fixture locate, origin/WCS picks) and the MCP pick tools call. No page carries its own picking rules.

title: Post gate refuses a Bore at a STEP hole's own size: the sim charges the 0.02 mm facet sagitta as a 20 mm gouge

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
A Bore on a modelled hole, at the hole's own size, is refused by the post gate as a **20 mm gouge**. The operation's own verify finds nothing. The overcut being charged is the gap between the true circle the bore cuts and the inscribed facets of the imported mesh, about 0.02 mm sideways.

**Reproduction** (main b57f8d52, Windows, `camcraft-cli mcp`):

```
import_model   {"path":"testdata/models/Milling-test.step","name":"part"}
set_stock      {"from_model":"part"}
add_tool       {"catalog":"EM-1000-4FL"}
add_operation  {"kind":"bore","tool":"EM-1000-4FL","source":"part","name":"OP"}
detect_holes   {"name":"OP"}        -> 1 hole: xy (0, 0), radius 12.5, entry z 20, floor z 0
generate       {"name":"OP"}        -> status ok, 0 warnings
verify         {}
```

`verify` returns no per-op finding. The program gate says:

```
gouge: program cuts below the model in 1 cell(s), worst 20.00 mm at (4.69, 11.59, z 0.00)
```

(4.69, 11.59) is at r = 12.50, on the hole wall. The same happens with EM-0800-4FL (1 cell, 20.00 mm at (11.76, -4.23)) and EM-0600-4FL (4 cells, 20.00 mm at (9.57, -8.04)).

**Neighbour cases that still work:**
- The same bore with `"stock_to_leave": 0.01` verifies clean, and so do 0.015, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5. With 0.005 it is still refused.
- A 2D Contour around the part's outside (convex walls) on the same finished-part setup passes the gate.

**Root cause (likely):** the STEP mesh is coarser than the gouge verdict.
- `list_features` on the part shows the Ø25 hole wall as 53 flat strips, 6.79° each. The chord sagitta is 12.5 × (1 − cos 3.40°) = **0.022 mm**.
- The STEP importer meshes to a chord tolerance of `extent * 1e-3` (`crates/app/src/geometry/import/step.rs`, `tol_target`), about 0.06 mm for this 60 mm part.
- The program sim judges against those facets with `tol` = `GOUGE_TOL` = 0.01 mm (`crates/sim/src/stock_sim/deviate.rs`, `deviate`). The sideways slack from #299 (`wall_slack.rs`) is the same 0.01 mm.
- On a concave curved wall the facets lie inside the true surface. A bore that cuts the true r = 12.5 therefore removes up to 0.022 mm of "model" between chord and arc. That is past the 0.01 slack, so the column is charged the wall's full 20 mm height.

The sagitta (0.022) against the threshold (stock_to_leave 0.01 plus tol 0.01) matches where the refusal stops. That is why this says "likely" and not "confirmed".

Any finishing pass that meets a concave curved wall at nominal size should hit the same thing: bores, a contour inside a round boss pocket, round internal corners. A larger part has a coarser mesh (extent/1000), so its sagitta is larger.

Done means: a bore at a STEP hole's nominal size verifies clean, a bore 0.05 mm oversize into the same wall is still refused, and both are pinned by tests.

body:
**Subscribe to this issue** (the "Subscribe" button on the right) if you work from a fork of CamCraft, especially with an AI agent.

Forks sync product code only at release tags (AGENTS.md "A fork syncs from upstream at each cut tag"). But the *process* - `AGENTS.md`, the agent definitions in `.claude/agents/`, the skills in `.claude/skills/` and `scripts/gate.*` - changes between releases, and a fork's agents should follow the current rules (review labels, priority labels, release steps, and so on).

**How it works:**
- `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` holds one number. Every PR that changes a process file bumps it.
- Every such PR also adds a comment **here**: the new version, what changed, and what to pull. Subscribers get one notification per change.
- A fork's agent compares its `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` with upstream's at the start of each session and, if upstream is newer, pulls just the process files (AGENTS.md "Process files sync on every session"). Product code still waits for the next release tag.

**To pull by hand:**
```
git fetch upstream
git checkout upstream/main -- AGENTS.md .claude/agents .claude/skills .claude/PROCESS_VERSION scripts/gate.ps1 scripts/gate.sh
git commit -m "chore(process): sync process files to upstream PROCESS_VERSION <n>"
```

This issue stays open and pinned. It's labelled `P?` so no agent ever picks it up as work.

title: Plasma: verification laws for through-cuts - kerf crossing, cut order, rapids, 2D gouge (part of #621)

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:max
labels.description: New algorithms, formats or open design (issue-worker-max)

body:
**Plasma verification laws: what replaces the gouge and collision checks for a through-cut.**

From [UM10720](https://tormach.com/media/asset/u/m/um10720_1300pl_1223a_web.pdf) §1.4.2, §4.12.8, §4.13 and the LinuxCNC Plasma Primer §12:
- **Kerf crossing.** A cut path that crosses an already-cut kerf or void (THC dives into the gap, which "can smash the torch into the material") is warned, naming the contour and point. A rapid across a cut-out part's area is warned too (tip-up hazard).
- **Cut order.** A part's inner contours must be cut before the outer that frees it. A violation is refused by name.
- **Rapids.** Rapids run at the operator's G30 Z (no CAM Z). The post must emit G30 after every M205; a missing G30 is a post bug that the law catches.
- **Kerf against the part.** The kerf-offset path must not cut into the part's material, which is the 2D gouge (part geometry versus the kerf band).
- **The 3D stock sim** doesn't run for plasma ops. The verdict is the 2D laws above, stated as such and not silently skipped.

**Done means:** each law is pinned with a fixture that trips it and one that passes; the program verdict blocks the post on a refusal (Prime Directive).

Part of #621

title: M7.3: carried stock (the two-sided Body) on the field engine - prerequisite for #586/#589

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:max
labels.description: New algorithms, formats or open design (issue-worker-max)

body:
Found while working #586 (M7.3 3/6). Part of #26.

**Why #586 can't finish as a seam move:** every app stock *holder* is either a plain grid or the **carried `Body`** (`crates/sim/src/stock_sim/carry.rs`). `Body` stores the stock carried between setups as **two-sided columns**: `pub dex: Dexel` plus a per-column floor (`on_floor` / `on_mesh`). It supports the setup-change transforms that `LatticeTurn` makes exact on a lattice: XY quarter turns, Z flips and mirrors (`carry`, `deviate`'s Z-mirror via `Dexel::from_grid`, `display()`).

The app also **mutates** it as a column store:
- `simulate(&mut body.dex, ..)` in `rest/across.rs` and `rest.rs`;
- `stock_sim_carry`'s clip loop writing `dex.lower(..)`;
- `Held::Plain(Dexel)` / `Held::Carried(Body)` and `dex_mut()`.

Swapping `Dexel` for `Stock` there is a **data-model change**: carried stock on the field engine.

**Open design questions:**
1. **Representation:** the field engine holds a solid as a narrow-band SDF plus cut layers. Carrying it is a rigid transform of the field (a re-sample, or a transformed query frame) rather than a lattice permutation. Is a transformed query frame (no re-sample) exact enough for the verdicts?
2. **Floors:** a flipped part's floor is the former top. The field is a closed solid, so it has no separate floor, but "a column cut through" needs an equivalent read.
3. **Clipping** to a later setup's own stock: a field intersection (max of SDFs) replaces `lower`.
4. **Equivalence:** a heavy-lane agreement test of the carried verdicts (`setup_carry`, `rest_across_setups`, `carried_verify`) on both engines, like `stock_engine_agreement`.

**Done means:** `stock_sim_carry`, `rest`, `rest/across` and the operation priors hold carried stock as `Stock`. A field-engine carry passes the same carried-stock suites, plus an agreement lane against the column carry. #586 can then close. This is a prerequisite of #589.

title: Locate the part in an imported fixture (or the fixture on the part) from the fixture and model pages

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Reported by the maintainer (filed by an agent), 2026-11-09: "we can import fixture. But we have no way of locating a part in the fixture on the fixture page or on the model page."

Part of #339 (fixtures/vises). Since #476/#549, a fixture's real mesh can be imported and is judged for collisions, but there's no way to put the part *in* it: the part and the fixture each sit where their files put them, so the collision verdict is only as good as that accidental placement.

**What's needed** (on the fixture page and the model page, the same tools both ways round):
1. **Mate by picks:** pick a face or point on the part, then the matching face or point on the fixture (a jaw face, a floor or parallel, a stop or locator pin). The part moves so the two coincide, with face normals opposed (part face sitting on the fixture face). Two or three mates fully locate it, the shop's 3-2-1 against a vise: the floor, the fixed jaw, then the stop.
2. **Numeric offset:** after a mate, nudge X/Y/Z (and a turn about the mate normal) by typed values. For example: 5 mm above the parallels, or 10 mm in from the stop.
3. **Move which one:** move the part into the fixture (default), or the fixture onto the part (common when the part is already aligned to the setup's plane, #330/#557, and the vise has to come to it).

**Rules:**
- **Commands:** every placement is one undoable command (`LocatePart` / `LocateFixture`), validated at creation and refused by name. That covers non-finite input, a degenerate pick (zero-area face, coincident points), a mate whose normals can't oppose, a placement that would leave the part interpenetrating the fixture (or at least warn by name), and no fixture or no model.
- **Frame:** the placement is relative to the setup the fixture belongs to. The setup's WCS (G54-G59, one per setup) is unchanged unless the user re-picks it. Stock follows the part as with part alignment (#326/#341).
- **Staleness:** moving the part or fixture marks that setup's ops stale (the collision verdict and toolpaths depend on it). Undo un-stales.

title: Trochoidal toolpaths: constant-engagement loops for slots, channels and corners (Adaptive mode + standalone op)

labels.name: claimed
labels.description: An agent is working on this - see the claim comment

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:max
labels.description: New algorithms, formats or open design (issue-worker-max)

body:
## What

A **trochoidal toolpath strategy**: circular loops whose centre advances along the cut. It's the usual constant-engagement way to clear slots, narrow channels and corners, where a spiral or offset adaptive path would be forced into full-width (or a sudden jump in) radial engagement. Ship it as a selectable option for Adaptive clearing (2D and 3D levels), and as a standalone "Trochoidal slot" operation along a chain or centre line.

This is a feature request. The existing trochoid work (#5, #47, the M11.4 fallbacks) only covers Adaptive's *internal* fallback in slot-width channels and thin bands. This issue is the general, user-facing strategy.

## Background (public literature)

- **Geometry**, for a simple circular loop: x(φ) = B·cos φ, y(φ) = B·sin φ + S·φ/(2π), with B the loop radius and S the forward advance per revolution. For a slot of width W cut by a tool of diameter D, B = (W − D)/2. Epicycloidal and double-trochoid variants also exist.
- **Engagement angle** θ = θ_out − θ_in: the centre angle of the cutter's contact arc with the *current* stock, read at each point along the path.
- **Chip thickness** in the peripheral approximation is h(α) = f_z·sin α. On a trochoid the engagement window moves along the loop, so h varies; it isn't constant.
- **How constant engagement is kept:** evaluate θ against the live stock, and when it exceeds the limit, shrink the loop, cut the forward step, or reshape the loop, and/or drop the feed where θ rises.
- **References:**
  - Otkur & Lazoglu, "Trochoidal milling", IJMTM 2007: chip-thickness and force model, double trochoid.
  - Rauch, Duc & Hascoet, "Improving trochoidal tool paths generation and implementation using process constraints modelling", IJMTM 2009.
  - B-spline trochoid optimisation with a maximum-engagement constraint, Int J Adv Manuf Technol 2022 (doi 10.1007/s00170-022-09527-z).
  - Circular, trochoidal and epicycloidal parameterisations, Prod. Eng. 2021 (doi 10.1007/s11740-021-01060-4).

## Proposed parameters (user parameters with defaults)

- loop width (≤ the channel width − D, auto from the channel when unset)
- forward step per loop
- maximum engagement angle (or the equivalent optimal load)
- return arc: cutting / non-cutting with microlift (height) / retract
- feed on the cutting arc vs the return arc (the return arc at a higher "air" feed)
- direction: climb / conventional
- smoothing radius for the loop-to-loop transitions

## Done means

1. A trochoid generator in `crates/motion` that is engagement-controlled against the in-process stock: the loop and step adapt so θ ≤ the limit everywhere, and a refusal by name where the channel is narrower than the tool or the limit can't be met.
2. Adaptive gets a "trochoidal in slots/corners" mode that switches from the spiral to trochoidal loops where the spiral would exceed the limit (merges with, or replaces, #5's internal fallback).
3. A standalone Trochoidal slot operation along a picked chain or centre line, through `CreateOperation` / `EditOperationParams` with undo.
4. The verifier judges the loops: no gouge, the engagement limit holds (a measured θ trace in tests), and microlift returns land on air (#47).
5. Pins:
   - a full-width slot with θ_max under the limit, compared with a straight slot at 180°;
   - a corner that a spiral path overloads, cut within the limit;
   - a too-narrow channel refused by name;
   - post goldens on Fanuc, where arcs are written as G2/G3 when the post supports them.

Related: #5, #7, #44, #47 (Adaptive trochoid internals).
